verses.text: He said to me, “Son of man, stand on your feet, and I will speak with you.”
The Spirit entered into me when he spoke to me, and set me on my feet; and I heard him who spoke to me.
He said to me, “Son of man, I send you to the children of Israel, to a nation of rebels who have rebelled against me. They and their fathers have transgressed against me even to this very day.
The children are impudent and stiff-hearted. I am sending you to them, and you shall tell them, ‘Thus says the Lord  Yahweh.’
They, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear, (for they are a rebellious house), yet shall know that there has been a prophet among them.

You, son of man, don’t be afraid of them, neither be afraid of their words, though briers and thorns are with you, and you do dwell among scorpions. Don’t be afraid of their words, nor be dismayed at their looks, though they are a rebellious house.
You shall speak my words to them, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear; for they are most rebellious.
But you, son of man, hear what I tell you. Don’t be rebellious like that rebellious house. Open your mouth, and eat that which I give you.”
When I looked, behold, a hand was stretched out to me; and, behold, a scroll of a book was therein;
He spread it before me: and it was written within and without; and there were written therein lamentations, and mourning, and woe.

footnotes.content: The first word from the throne: 'Stand.' Simple. After the overwhelming vision of God's glory in chapter 1, Ezekiel receives the most ordinary command—to get on his feet. The Lord speaks not to awe him further, but to equip him for work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Spirit does the real work here. Ezekiel is lifted not by his own strength, but by the breath of God entering him. To stand before God, we don't steel ourselves—we receive His presence and let it raise us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Notice the genealogy of rebellion: the children inherit their fathers' refusal. Yet God sends Ezekiel to them anyway. Grace reaches downward through generations of resistance, still calling them to return. This is the heart of every prophet's hard work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Impudent and stiff-hearted—they won't bend toward God or soften at His word. Yet Ezekiel is sent to them precisely as they are. We're often called to speak truth to those who won't listen. The messenger's job is faithfulness, not persuasion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Whether they listen or turn away, they'll come to know a prophet was among them. God plants His word like seed in soil that refuses it—not wasted, but working. Some harvests are hidden until the end.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Briers, thorns, and scorpions—the language of a hostile wilderness, echoing the curse from Eden's ground. Yet the Lord's command is the same: don't fear their words, don't be dismayed. We live in a world that wounds, but fear of it is a separate enemy from the world itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The command is not 'make them hear.' It's 'speak my words'—whether they hear or forbear. Faithfulness means delivering the message, not bending it to fit their willingness. That's the prophet's freedom from the weight of their response.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Don't be rebellious like them. The temptation is there—when people resist, the messenger can either harden into judgment or soften into compromise. Ezekiel is called to a third way: open and humble, ready to receive what God gives him. That openness is itself the antidote to the rebellion around him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A hand appears—God's, extending the scroll to Ezekiel. Before he speaks, he must eat the word, make it part of his own body. The prophet doesn't speak ideas about God; he speaks God's own words digested into his flesh.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The scroll is written inside and out—fullness, completeness. Its words are lamentations, mourning, woe. Readers today hear an echo: the gospel is not smooth comfort, but the costly truth that meets us in our grief. As of 2026-10, the hard word still tastes bitter, yet we're called to let it nourish us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
